Affine combinations are currently implemented using choice:

def affineCombination (p : ι → P) : (ι → k) →ᵃ[k] P where
  toFun w := s.weightedVSubOfPoint p (Classical.choice S.nonempty) w +ᵥ Classical.choice S.nonempty
  ...

This forces noncomputable here and in unexpected places downstream, and causes further problems such as in convexity (@Yaël Dillies)

/-- Any affine space is a convex space.

This is not an instance because its convex combination operation is defined through the choice of an
arbitrary basepoint, which makes it very diamond-prone. -/
def toConvexSpace : ConvexSpace R P where ...

I propose a reworking of affine combinations based on affine homogenization as implemented in PR #39431 by @Attila Gáspár. I am using this PR already for convexity theory and am quite in favor of it. Note that it is computable!

The idea is to compute an affine combination, we embed the affine space in its canonical homogenization, compute a linear combination using the given coefficients, and pull back the result to the affine space. As far as I understand this, this should be computable. I don't know how nicely this will unpack for defeq purposes, but I have some hope that we can optimize for this.

I want to gather opinions on this before I consider working on this since it will require quite some work on affine spaces and maps to make this smooth.
you would need to change one of the pi arguments to a finsupp I think
and you would also have to require the sum be one
otherwise I see no way it could possibly be computable

Aaron Liu said:

and you would also have to require the sum be one

Yes, indeed. In fact, I envision a structure AffineCoeff in analogy to Convexity.StdSimplex to be used for coefficients.

Something like this perhaps

def affineCombination : AffineCoeff k P →ᵃ[k] P where ...
Maybe rename AffineCoeff to BarycentricCoord?

Weiyi Wang said:

Maybe rename AffineCoeff to BarycentricCoord?

I am of course open to discussing the naming. Im principle, Coord is fine for me. I see the need for three types of coefficient structures:

  • SumOneCoeff or AffineCoeff which requires the sum to be 1
  • SumZeroCoeff which requires the sum to be 0 (this will be the underlying linear space over which AffineCoeff is the affine space)
  • ConvexCoeff extends AffineCoeff by nonnegativity constraints. This is the same as StdSimplex, which should perhaps be renamed for sake of consistency.

Choosing consistent names throughout would be desirable.

For naming we should consider what other parts of mathlib might want to use this structure. I can think of probability distributions and partitions of unity. Neither of them would call these "coordinates". Not sure "coefficient" is better though.
By the way, In principle, AffineCoeff/Coord allows for the possibility to implement an abstract AffineSpace in analogy to the current abstract ConvexSpace (not that I intend to do so at this time).

I don't think computability would help with the ConvexSpace diamond. If we consider the product of two affine spaces, then the convex combination could be computed either using some generic instance for AddTorsor, or by computing it componentwise. But even if we implemented the instance for AddTorsor in a computable way, it would still use recursion on the coefficients without using the product structure, so it wouldn't reduce to Prod.mk.

Also, my implementation of the homogenization doesn't yet have a computable way of turning an affine combination in the homogenization back into a point in the original affine space, so it's not clear to me how computability helps in your use case.

There's another issue with computability: if we implement the homogenization for abstract affine spaces, then Homogenization.ofVector cannot be computable (or at least I couldn't find a way to implement it). Maybe we could have both implementations and noncomputable functions for converting between them, but it seems to be unnecessary duplication, since apart from computability, one of them is strictly more general.

I believe this. The docstring of toConvexSpace should probably be changed if choice is not the primary blocker.

Attila Gáspár said:

Also, my implementation of the homogenization doesn't yet have a computable way of turning an affine combination in the homogenization back into a point in the original affine space, so it's not clear to me how computability helps in your use case.

I believe this should be possible. There is an obvious isomorphism from P to toPoint.range (if AffineMap.range would exist). The identity is an isomorphism from ofPoint.range to comap weight {1} ({1} interpreted as an affine subspace). It seems to me that affine combinations on comap weight {1} are easy to describe computably since they are just linear combinations.
@Martin Winter I've implemented the computable equivalences here.
affineCombination, weightedVSub and weightedVSubOfPoint all go together, any refactoring would need to be applied to all three definitions at once.

In principle it makes sense for those definitions to operate on Finsupp (with or without the extra constraints on coefficients summing to 1 for affineCombination and 0 for weightedVSub). In practice, I've always found the API for sums over Finset to be much more intuitive and easy to work with than the API for sums over Finsupp.

So the key test there is whether proofs involving those definitions (especially those currently involving moving between summation over different Finsets or types) become simpler or more complicated. And similarly whether requiring weights to be constructed with a proof that the sum is 1 or 0, rather than deferring such proof obligations until needed later, makes things more complicated, or whether in practice a limited set of constructors suffices to produce all the weights needed in practice, with the type that ensures the correct sum.

I think it's very unlikely that computability matters here at all; we don't design things in mathlib to be computable, we use tactics for computation as needed. And none of this would plausibly help defeq issues for convex spaces, those would need appropriate Prop typeclasses to assert that the convex space instance equals that given by the module or torsor structure.

Note that the space of coordinates for affine combinations already exists as an AffineSubspace in the form of fintypeAffineCoords and finsuppAffineCoords, although quite possibly there's a use for having a separate type for this and just defining affine equivalences to the AffineSubspace versions.

Joseph Myers said:

Note that the space of coordinates for affine combinations already exists as an AffineSubspace in the form of fintypeAffineCoords and finsuppAffineCoords, although quite possibly there's a use for having a separate type for this and just defining affine equivalences to the AffineSubspace versions.

This is good to know! Is there a reason we have two?
A Finsupp version is more general, but if you have a finite index type then it's always going to be more convenient to work directly with Pi types than with (equivalent) Finsupp.
